results.title: Why Big Tech's $828 Billion Infrastructure Bill Will Hit Your API Invoice
results.description: Friday's market session wiped out more than one trillion dollars in market value across the Nasdaq 100. The immediate catalyst was the cumulative disclosure from the third-quarter earnings cycle. Five tech operators, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and SpaceX with xAI, are set to deploy eight hundred and twenty-eight billion dollars in capital expenditures in 2026 alone. For context, that annual infrastructure check approaches the entire annual defense budget of the United States. Wall Street spent twenty years bidding up software multiples because the business model was asset-light. A firm wrote code once, deployed it across shared racks, and collected eighty percent gross margins. Operating cash flows compounded internally, funding share buybacks and dividend growth without needing to tap debt capital markets. That corporate cash flywheel broke in the third quarter. Four of the five major compute spenders recorded negative free cash flow. Amazon burned through forty-two billion dollars in negative free cash flow over the trailing twelve months. Meta swung to negative two billion dollars in quarterly free cash flow and filed plans to raise up to ninety-five billion dollars in equity. Even Microsoft, the lone provider maintaining positive operating free cash flow, issued twenty-five billion dollars in corporate bonds, its first debt offering in more than nine years. Andy Jassy summarized the corporate defense on Amazon's earnings call by noting that while spreading this capital expenditure over twenty-five years might be convenient, the current technological window does not permit that schedule. That logic explains the competitive terror driving the buildout. When every frontier competitor believes that failing to procure gigawatts today forfeits the next platform layer, spending becomes non-discretionary. What the earnings transcripts omit is the asset-liability duration mismatch created when three-year depreciating assets are funded with long-term capital. A power utility spends tens of billions of dollars on physical infrastructure, but it does so under a regulated rate base. Regulators grant utilities guaranteed returns on equity in exchange for serving captive rate payers. Silicon Valley hyperscalers are building out utility-scale physical grids, substations, and chilled water loops without any regulatory return guarantee. They bear full merchant risk on silicon accelerators that suffer fifty percent economic obsolescence every eighteen to twenty-four months as next-generation clusters deliver higher FLOPs per watt. That capital intensity shifts the economic burden directly onto downstream software engineering teams and enterprise buyers. When cloud platforms operated on surplus operating cash flow, they could afford to offer loss-leading inference pricing to acquire developer distribution. Token subsidies made sense as customer acquisition cost while the underlying software margins stayed wide. With four out of five providers posting negative free cash flow and servicing new bond coupons, compute infrastructure must generate cash returns. The eight hundred and twenty-eight billion dollar buildout guarantees that cloud providers cannot keep API token rates artificially depressed beneath their full depreciation load. If a hyperscaler must service twenty-five billion dollars in corporate debt and justify ninety-five billion dollars in prospective equity dilution, the realized carrying cost of those GPU clusters must clear through monthly compute invoices. Engineering teams building autonomous multi-step agent pipelines under the assumption that compute pricing will decline toward zero will find their operating margins squeezed between rising token consumption and cloud providers who need to service hard capital obligations.

results.title: Waterfowl hunters urged to take precautions on lower Arkansas River following Pueblo sewage spill
results.description: Waterfowl hunters urged to take precautions on lower Arkansas River following Pueblo sewage spill mps-post Sat, 10/31/2026 - 10:22 (Kiowa County Press) Colorado Parks and Wildlife is urging waterfowl hunters to take care along the Arkansas River and nearby state wildlife areas. A sewage spill in Pueblo earlier this year may have left the water unsafe. The warning comes as waterfowl hunting season gets underway in southeastern Colorado. It also applies to other people who spend time outdoors along the river. The spill took place August 26-27. It released about 4.2 million gallons of untreated sewage into the Arkansas River. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment then tested the water. It found high levels of E. coli bacteria at several places downstream. Water quality has improved in some places. In other stretches of the river, high bacteria levels have stayed. Bacteria levels have also risen for short periods after rain. Rain washes waste from nearby areas into the water. These changes show why people should know local water conditions and take care. The health department has tested the river many times. The latest sampling and test results are available online. Waterfowl hunters face added risk. They often wade into shallow water and retrieve the birds they shoot. They also handle wet gear and carry clothing and equipment that may have touched river water or mud. "Raw sewage can carry pathogens such as E. coli, viruses and parasites," said Ashley Rust, Ph.D., CPW water quality specialist. "Out of an abundance of caution, we provide these advisories to the public." Colorado Parks and Wildlife recommends these steps for hunters near water that may be contaminated. Avoid direct water contact. Stay out of waters under active contact advisories. Do not expose bare skin to water or mud that may be contaminated. This is especially important for open cuts or wounds. Clean clothing and footwear. Take off wet clothing and footwear after hunting. Wash those clothes by themselves with detergent and dry them fully. Clean boots and waders before storing or using them again. Clean hunting equipment. Fully clean decoys, retrieval gear and other equipment that may have touched the water or mud. Keep dirty gear away from food, clean clothing and personal items. Wash hands and exposed skin. Use soap and clean running water. Wash hands for at least 20 seconds after touching water, mud, hunting gear or harvested birds. Also wash before eating or preparing food. Scrub between fingers and under fingernails. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends soap and water over hand sanitizer. Washing physically removes germs and dirt that sanitizer may not kill. If soap and water are not available, use hand sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol until you can wash properly. Handle harvested waterfowl carefully. Wear disposable gloves when cleaning birds. Keep game clean, cool and dry. Do not let contaminated water or equipment touch the meat. Practice safe food preparation. Wash hands, knives, cutting boards and work surfaces after handling raw game. Keep raw meat away from other foods. Cook game meat to an inside temperature of at least 165 degrees Fahrenheit. Leaving the field. Hunters should think about carrying clean water, soap and paper towels in their vehicles or gear. That way they can wash their hands before eating, handling food or leaving the field. Retriever dogs. Hunters who use dogs should plan to rinse them with clean water. They should also try to keep dogs from drinking water that may be contaminated. Dogs and other pets can be exposed to harmful bacteria by touching or drinking contaminated water. "These additional precautions may require hunters to take a few extra steps before, during and after their time in the field, but they should complement, never distract from, the basic safety practices every hunter should follow," said Mike Brown, Colorado Parks and Wildlife Pueblo area wildlife manager. "Safe firearm handling, knowing your target and what lies beyond it, wearing a life jacket when hunting from a boat, remaining aware of changing weather and water conditions, and carrying your hunting license are just as important today as ever. We want hunters to enjoy the season, protect themselves and return home safely." The agency issued a water contact advisory on September 2. It named 10 state wildlife areas and the Las Animas Fish Hatchery along the Arkansas River as possibly affected by the spill. The wildlife areas named were Melon Valley, Rocky Ford, Oxbow, Purgatoire River, Fort Lyon, North Gateway Ponds, Granada, Deadman, Midwestern Farms and Holly. Water quality has varied along the river since the spill. On September 4, Colorado Parks and Wildlife lifted the sewage-related advisory at John Martin Reservoir State Park. Repeated tests showed the water there met standards for recreation. Hunters and other visitors should not assume the whole river is safe because one location has improved. They are encouraged to check the latest water quality information from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. They should also follow any posted advisories before entering affected areas. results.title: 'Way Out Of Shape!': Trump Attacks Reporter's Weight In Bizarre Tarmac Meltdown
results.description: Donald Trump berated a Reuters reporter for asking him pertinent questions during his midterm rally push. REUTERS: So, you not going to Kansas has nothing to do with you being sick of travel? TRUMP: Oh, you're sick to ask that question. You are sick. Who you with? REUTERS: I'm with Reuters, sir. TRUMP: You are a sick guy. Reuters is terrible, by the way. Can you imagine? REUTERS:Well, we just want to make sure you're doing well. TRUMP: Look at this guy. He's way out of shape. Look at how badly... He comes to me. REUTERS: Sir, you're not going to go to Kansas. TRUMP: I'm not going to Kansas because he's doing very well. I'm going to do a tele-rounding. Tomorrow, I'm doing Florida. He said, what's the reason? After doing, what, 28? He says, what's the reason for this? Sir, that you're not going to Kansas. You know what the reason is? I don't feel I have to go to Kansas. I'm going to Florida tomorrow, and I'll do...If something else comes up. But he said, you're not going to Kansas, sir. Are you feeling well? You've been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell. How's that hand doing? Still rotting away? Get on a scale, Donald.

results.title: Mystery Hormuz Attack: Iran Says Fishermen Hit By ‘Enemy Drone’ As US Hellfire Claim Emerges
results.description: Iranian fishing boats have reportedly come under attack near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, but sharply conflicting accounts have emerged over what happened and the casualties. Iran’s Fars News says two fishing boats were struck in what it described as an “enemy drone attack,” leaving two fishermen missing and two wounded. The supplied Iranian material does not identify the aircraft responsible. A separate, unverified account goes considerably further, claiming the fishermen approached and filmed two US AH-64E Apache attack helicopters before an American MQ-1C armed drone intervened and fired two AGM-114 Hellfire missiles at the boats. That account claims four fishermen were killed. These details and casualty figures have not been established in the supplied material. What the accounts share is a potentially dangerous development: Iranian fishing vessels were reportedly attacked near Qeshm, adding another flashpoint to the increasingly tense waters of Hormuz.
